title: What is a parallel stream, how does it use the ForkJoinPool, and what are its caveats (ordering, small datasets, shared mutable state)?
shortTitle: Parallel stream: ForkJoinPool, when to use, caveats (ordering, small data, shared state)
keyPoints: parallelStream() splits the source using Spliterator.trySplit() and processes partitions on ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
Default parallelism is availableProcessors minus 1 worker threads plus the caller thread.
All parallel streams in the JVM share ONE common ForkJoinPool: a slow pipeline blocks others.
Use a custom ForkJoinPool to isolate critical pipelines from the shared common pool.
Parallel streams are only beneficial for large datasets (10K+ elements) with CPU-bound per-element work.
forEach in parallel produces scrambled output; use forEachOrdered or toList() for ordered results.
ArrayList and arrays split evenly in O(1); LinkedList requires O(n) traversal to split, making parallel inefficient.

s1_definition.oneliner: A parallel stream splits data into partitions processed by ForkJoinPool threads, beneficial for large CPU-bound datasets but harmful for small data, I/O-bound work, shared state, and order-sensitive operations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Mechanism**: `parallelStream()` or `stream().parallel()` uses `Spliterator.trySplit()` to divide data into partitions processed by the common ForkJoinPool.
- **Thread count**: `availableProcessors() - 1` worker threads plus the caller thread.
- **Shared pool**: all parallel streams in the JVM share one ForkJoinPool; a slow stream blocks others.
- **Custom pool**: `new ForkJoinPool(n).submit(() -> stream...).get()` isolates critical pipelines.
- **When beneficial**: 10K+ elements, CPU-bound work, independent elements, well-splittable source (ArrayList, array).
- **When harmful**: small datasets, I/O-bound, shared mutable state, LinkedList, order-critical forEach.
s1_definition.analogy: A sequential stream is one clerk processing 10,000 cheques at National Bank of India. A parallel stream is 8 clerks each taking approximately 1,250 cheques, processing simultaneously, then combining results. Fast for 10,000 cheques. But for only 10 cheques, hiring 8 clerks is overhead for no benefit. If all 8 clerks write to the same ledger simultaneously, entries get lost. All departments share the same pool of clerks: if accounting hogs them, loan processing waits.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Parallel Stream Pipeline:
  ─────────────────────────
  Source: [T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6, T7, T8]
           │
  trySplit: [T1-T4] → Thread-1    [T5-T8] → Thread-2
           │                         │
  filter+map per partition          filter+map per partition
           │                         │
  reduce locally                    reduce locally
           │                         │
           └──────── merge ──────────┘
                       │
                    Result

  Common Pool (shared!):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ parallel stream A (slow)        │ blocks
  │ parallel stream B (fast)        │ waits!
  │ parallel stream C               │ waits!
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
  Fix: custom ForkJoinPool per critical pipeline
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A parallel stream splits data into partitions processed by ForkJoinPool threads, providing near-linear speedup for CPU-bound operations on large datasets. The six caveats are ordering, small datasets, shared mutable state, common pool starvation, poor source splittability, and I/O-bound work.

The decision: use parallel streams for 10K+ elements with CPU-bound work on well-splittable sources. Avoid for small datasets, I/O-bound work, and shared state. Use custom ForkJoinPool for production pipelines.

Remember one sentence: parallel streams split data across ForkJoinPool threads and are only faster for large CPU-bound datasets with independent elements.
